eligibility_note: Own panel estimation (PSCC-FE, IV-GMM, SQREG); mobile and fixed telephone subscriptions (ICT/mobile); stated 193 countries (152/151 groups estimated) with explicit income-group comparison (Tables 8-9); outcome HDI (living standards beyond income).

results.quote: lnMOB exerts a positive and statistical effect at the 1% level

results.correction: Direction and numbers match Table 6 (cols 3-4 0.00708, 0.00673; col 2 -0.860, t -1.059; Hansen 0.319). Note col 2 sign is negative and insignificant, so 'positive' holds only when IQI is in the model.
Numbers match Table 6 cols 5-7 (0.0659, 0.0194, 0.0193; t 6.686, 12.23, 12.28). Sign opposite to Table 5 col 5-7 is real.
Matches Table 7 mobile panel; fixed-telephone SQREG (0.0236, 0.0188, 0.0183 at Q25/50/75 w/o IQI) is not recorded.
Matches Table 8 mobile model; all four coefficients positive, only high (1%) and lower-middle (10%) significant.
Matches Table 9 mobile model; 'seven of eight models positive' is the authors' own count.

heterogeneity.quote: high- and lower-middle-income countries show significant positive outcomes, while the effect is negative for low-income countries regarding fixed telephones

heterogeneity.correction: Sign pattern of IQI holds for IV-GMM (Table 9: high +0.0828***, LM -0.132***, UM +0.125***; low mobile +0.133 ns) but NOT for PSCC-FE (Table 8 mobile: high +0.0605***, low +0.0589**, LM -0.0608**, UM -0.0525***; fixed: UM -0.0151 ns). The paper's text claim (positive in high/UM, negative in low/LM) contradicts Table 8. ICT x IQI interaction signs (IV-GMM: high -0.00373, UM -0.00692, LM +0.0106) are correct; low-income is -0.00939 ns (mobile) but +0.289*** (fixed), so 'narrows institution gap in poorer groups' is not uniform.
Matches Table 7; 0.0062-0.0076 is the no-interaction specification, with interaction the Q75 estimate is 0.00933 (Q50 0.00540).

income_group_note: All listed high/UM/LM/low coefficients and significance levels match Tables 8-9 (incl. low-income fixed IV-GMM 0.886***, R2 -7.735, no year dummies). Sample counts per group (47/25/39/41) match Table 8.

risk_of_bias.confounding_reverse_causation: agree: causal language, only one-period lags and an IV-GMM whose instruments are never described; Hansen p near 0.05 in some groups.
risk_of_bias.exposure_measurement: agree: logs of absolute subscription counts (mean 35.4 million, max 1.75e9) track population, not penetration; telephony is narrow ICT.
risk_of_bias.selection_of_countries_years: agree: ~150 of 193 countries used, unbalanced, 10 years; duplicate Congo, Dem. Rep. rows 39-40 in Table A1.
risk_of_bias.outcome_measurement: agree: HDI is a slow-moving composite and a loose proxy for 'inclusive growth', but fits living standards beyond income.
risk_of_bias.specification: agree: many specifications, sign flip for fixed telephones across estimators, implausible low-income IV-GMM estimates and F-statistics of 10^6.
risk_of_bias.selective_reporting: agree: all models are tabulated but text overstates consistency (e.g. says Table 6 aligns with Table 5; text on IQI signs contradicts Table 8).
risk_of_bias.why: Panel associations with year dummies and lags, no credible reverse-causality strategy and a count-based exposure; serious is appropriate.

problems: Record is accurate on all numbers checked. Only substantive error: heterogeneity item 2 repeats the authors' text on IQI signs by income group, which contradicts Table 8 (see correction). Minor: Table 5 col 4 lnICT (0.0112, t 3.646) and Table 7 fixed-telephone SQREG not recorded. Record's stated Hansen values, group counts and Congo duplicate are correct.

eligibility_note: Own estimation (AMG then DOLS) on 17 EU countries x 13 manufacturing sectors, 1995-2007; exposure is sectoral ICT capital services (ICT in general, narrow measure); outcome TFP (output/productivity). Meets >=10 economies.

sample_corrections.income_groups_covered: Not reported in the paper; the 'high-income and some upper-middle-income' statement is the extractor's inference (paper only groups EU core/South/East).

results.correction: Estimates and t-values match Table 2 (0.06 (2.40), 0.07 (3.19), std. beta 0.07***). Text locator is p.416, not p.415 (sentence follows Table 2).
results.quote: ln ICT 0.06 (2.40) 0.07 (3.19) 0.07***; 'a more intensive use of ICT leads to an improvement in TFP'

heterogeneity.quote: our sample is not sufficiently large and hence we do not have enough degrees of freedom for this approach

income_group_note: Paper reports no income-group results; core/South/East groups are used descriptively for TFP levels only. Record's 'not reported' entries are correct.

risk_of_bias.confounding_reverse_causation: agree: DOLS leads/lags only; the claim that cointegration means 'omitted variables cannot impact TFP' is not valid, no instrument.
risk_of_bias.exposure_measurement: agree: ICT capital services contribution to VA growth is a sensible sectoral proxy, though a growth contribution entered in logs and compared with TFP levels is unusual.
risk_of_bias.selection_of_countries_years: agree: data-availability sample; Hungary/Czech anomaly kept (note 21 says exclusion run but not shown); Portugal appears in the South group text but not in Table 1.
risk_of_bias.outcome_measurement: too_harsh: TFP as an AMG production-function residual is a standard (if generated) outcome; the generated-regressor and unexplained N=451 concerns justify moderate rather than serious.
risk_of_bias.specification: agree: two columns only, lead/lag length not reported; moderate.
risk_of_bias.selective_reporting: agree: differenced terms unreported and robustness without Hungary/Czech Republic mentioned but not shown.
risk_of_bias.why: Overall serious is right because identification rests on DOLS with an invalid omitted-variable argument, even if the outcome domain is a little harsh.

problems: No invented numbers. Corrections: income-group coverage statement is not in the text; ICT quote locator p.416. Table 2 N=451 confirmed (unexplained). Std. beta 0.07 is the smallest of the significant effects (HC 0.69, EF -0.11, ext. openness -0.25), consistent with the record.

eligibility_note: Own panel estimation on 136 countries 2000-2020 (N=2856, balanced); exposure internet users share (mobile as robustness); outcomes carbon productivity (GDP per unit CO2: productivity/resource cost) and top-10% income share (distribution); income-group split high/middle/low.

results.quote: For every 1% increase in digitization level, CP increases by 0.0687%

results.correction: Matches Table 10 col 2. Mediation shares 22.36% (R&D) and 26.34% (inequality) recompute correctly from the table.
Directions as stated in text; coefficients appear only in Fig. 5 (not in text), so magnitudes cannot be checked; Oceania significance not stated in text.
results.quote: In African countries, the impact of digitization on CP is not significant. In Oceanian countries, digitization has a negative effect on CP.

heterogeneity.quote: coefficients of digitization in high-income, middle-income, and low-income countries are 0.0849, 0.0579, and 0.0408 respectively, all significant at the 1% level
countries with high human capital levels, middle human capital levels, and low human capital levels are 0.0907, 0.0694, and 0.0429, respectively

heterogeneity.correction: Region and quantile statements supported by text and Table 11.
heterogeneity.quote: the promoting effect of digitization on CP is strongest in European countries

income_group_note: High 0.0849, middle 0.0579, low 0.0408, all p<0.01 per text; coefficients and SEs shown only in Fig. 6 (not extractable). Middle income is not split.

risk_of_bias.confounding_reverse_causation: agree: causal 'impact' language, country FE only (no year effects in Eq. 1), system GMM with Hansen p=1.000 and no instrument details.
risk_of_bias.exposure_measurement: agree: internet users share is a coarse proxy for 'digitization'; mobile penetration robustness is useful.
risk_of_bias.selection_of_countries_years: agree: 136 countries chosen for data completeness; intro says 163 countries once (inconsistency).
risk_of_bias.outcome_measurement: agree: GDP per CO2 is a ratio that moves with GDP; top-10% income share is standard; Table 1 not extractable to check sources.
risk_of_bias.specification: agree: coefficient rises from 0.0210 to 0.0687 with controls (cols 3-6), SE clustering unstated, preliminary tests not reflected in estimator choice.
risk_of_bias.selective_reporting: agree: heterogeneity shown only in figures; GMM estimate (about one third of FE) described as confirming robustness.
risk_of_bias.why: Fixed-effects associations with causal framing and a weak GMM check; serious is appropriate.

problems: No invented numbers found. Record's 'seven columns' stepwise description is loose (cols 1-2 are OLS/FE without controls, col 7 is RE). Table 1 (variable sources) is not in extracted text, so the 'World Bank territorial CO2' claim is unverifiable.

eligibility_note: Own estimation, 67 countries 1995-2019 (>=3 for AI). Borderline on two criteria: exposure is industrial robot stock per capita, labelled AI by authors who concede it is 'far from being a comprehensive indicator of AI'; outcome is carbon inequality (distribution of CO2 per capita between and within countries), a distribution/resource-cost outcome rather than income distribution. Kept as eligible on the authors' framing; flag as weak fit.

income_group_note: No income-group results; paper lists income comparison as future work.

risk_of_bias.confounding_reverse_causation: agree: causal language, internal-lag SYS-GMM and lagged-AI IV-GMM, Sargan p of 0.95-1.0000; authors admit reverse causality cannot be ruled out.
risk_of_bias.exposure_measurement: agree: industrial robot stock is automation in manufacturing, not AI generally.
risk_of_bias.selection_of_countries_years: agree: 67 (56 for GVC) countries chosen on IFR robot data, mainly 'countries with comparative advantages in AI development'.
risk_of_bias.outcome_measurement: agree: author-constructed CI_INTER (relative to 67-country mean) and WID-based CI_INTRA; dependent on sample composition.
risk_of_bias.specification: agree: effect sizes vary 100-fold across estimators, mixed I(0)/I(1) series (Table 4), implausible t-statistics (L.Y t = 1876.54, 1279.80).
risk_of_bias.selective_reporting: too_harsh: inconsistencies (0.00016% vs 0.0016; TRADE and GOV threshold numbers swapped in Sec 5.6 text; Table 8 L.Y negative t with positive coefficient; Eq. 6 lags CI_INTER; Sec 5.5 says 'inter-country' for governance) are real but look like reporting errors; all estimated models are tabulated, so moderate is fairer.
risk_of_bias.why: Dynamic-panel associations with a weak AI proxy and no credible exogeneity; serious holds even if reporting-errors domain is slightly harsh.

problems: All numbers in record match tables. Real defects in paper confirmed by text: 0.00016% vs 0.0016; Sec 5.6 text describes the TRADE column with GOV numbers (d -0.0078, net -0.0047; table col 1 d_LNAI is -0.0665) and the GOV column with the TRADE value (0.0031-0.0665); Table 11 d_Cons equals b_LNAI in every column; Table 8 L.Y t-statistics negative. Record correction: Tables 9 and 11 lack an N row (Table 10 does report N), so 'Tables 9-11 lack N' is slightly overstated. Result 3 duplicates results 1-2.
